paragraphs: The distinction between creator and creation is fundamental: no created being can take the creator’s place. The world belongs to the creator, who was, is, and always will be its ultimate owner. No creature can therefore claim ultimate ownership of the world, in whole or in part. Creation depends on the creator not only for its existence, but also for its purpose. It exists for the creator to express and extend its presence, and all meaning flows from this purpose. The world is ultimately about the creator, not any individual creature. Any created being’s attempt to take the creator’s place is usurpation; treating anything apart from the creator as the ultimate source of meaning gives it the devotion due to the creator alone and is therefore idolatry. Neither can fulfill creation’s purpose. The Ten Commandments affirm that worship belongs to God alone and forbid the worship of any created being [39].

Ultimate ownership belongs to the creator alone, yet legitimate human ownership remains a genuine right that helps sustain human life. Aquinas likewise distinguishes God’s sovereign dominion from lawful private ownership [51]. Human ownership is not ultimate, but this does not give any individual, institution, or government the right to seize another’s possessions merely by claiming to represent the creator. Even poor management does not grant another party the creator’s ultimate authority. Private ownership must therefore be protected, not absorbed by a state that treats its authority as unlimited [52]. At the same time, ownership carries responsibilities: owners should regard themselves as stewards of God’s providence, caring wisely for their possessions and using them to benefit their families and others [53]. Understood and exercised in this way, such ownership becomes a blessing.

The creator’s transcendence and central place do not diminish humanity’s significance; they give it direction. Our calling is not to claim ultimate ownership of the world or make ourselves its center, but to care responsibly for what we own and freely align our lives with the creator’s purpose. We need neither deny legitimate ownership nor mistake it for ultimate dominion. A meaningful life is one in which our possessions, freedom, and gifts serve this calling: to honor the creator’s likeness within us and extend the creator’s presence into the world.
